title: Microsoft’s Majorana 1 — Media Manipulation OR Scientific Breakthrough?
bodyHtml:
Microsoft’s Majorana 1 — Media Manipulation OR Scientific Breakthrough?

Backstory:
My peaceful life was disrupted on 19th Feb 2025, as Microsoft announced their Majorana 1 topological quantum computer; not because it was great or new or something exciting but because as a social quantum enthusiast all of my relatives, friends, and random strangers bombarded me with the same message! Big companies are bigger show-offs and their extravagant claims hidden behind complex terminologies needed to be decoded by this undergraduate with no expertise but just passion. So, here I present my findings…

Paper: Interferometric single-shot parity measurement in InAs–Al hybrid devices by Microsoft Azure Quantum

Note*: This is a highly technical ECE (Electronic & Computer Engineering) paper delving deep into quantum physics, mainly its application in measurement-only topological quantum computing so, I assume that by now you at least know about quantum computing and basic quantum physics (without mathematical understanding). If you have this knowledge then make sure you don’t get tangled up in terminologies and surf through them as I explain the key takeaways of the paper.

Pre-Paper Fundamentals: Topological Quantum Computing

The paper suggests a potential implementation of physicist Alexei Kitaev’s topological quantum computer idea & physicist Ettore Majorana’s theorized Majorana fermions. So, let’s dive into the pre-requisite topics to better understand what the paper is talking about.

The standard way we think about quantum computers involves initializing qubits (the basic units of quantum information), applying quantum gates (operations that manipulate these qubits), and then measuring the final state to get the result. Topological Quantum Computing (TQC) offers a different approach, where the fundamental idea is to use the exchange of identical particles as a way to perform quantum computations. This might seem strange, as we usually think of exchanging particles as just swapping their positions. However, in the quantum world, especially in systems with many identical particles, the act of exchanging particles can have profound consequences on the system’s quantum state. The way a particle’s quantum state changes upon exchange is described by its exchange statistics.

We are familiar with two basic types of particles: bosons and fermions. When two bosons are exchanged, the overall quantum state of the system remains unchanged. When two fermions are exchanged, the overall quantum state picks up a minus sign. These are the only possibilities for fundamental particles in three spatial dimensions. However, in two-dimensional systems, the possibilities for exchange statistics are richer. Here, particles can exist that are neither bosons nor fermions; these exotic particles are called anyons.

What’s special about them is that their exchange statistics can be more complex than just bosons or fermions. Think of it like different types of knots you can tie with strings in 2D versus 3D — more possibilities emerge in fewer dimensions. Among these anyons, there are two main types relevant to our story: Abelian anyons and non-Abelian anyons. Abelian anyons are a bit simpler; swapping them just adds a phase factor. But the real stars of the TQC show are non-Abelian anyons. When you exchange these, something much more powerful happens — it’s like performing a quantum gate. What makes this truly special is that the result of the computation depends on the overall pattern of these exchanges, a process called braiding. And because this depends on the fundamental way the paths intertwine — a topological property — it’s inherently more resistant to small errors.

One particularly promising type of non-Abelian anyon is linked to topological superconductors. These are special materials that can host peculiar excitations at their edges or defects called Majorana zero modes (MZMs). Our source tells us that Majorana zero modes are a type of non-Abelian anyon known as Ising anyons. The cool thing about braiding these MZMs is that you can perform certain protected quantum gates. For instance, swapping two MZMs can have a specific effect on a qubit encoded within a set of them. However, the plot thickens! While braiding Ising anyons is great for protected operations, it might not be enough to build a fully universal quantum computer — one that can do absolutely any calculation. For that, scientists have their eyes on another type of anyon called Fibonacci anyons, which are theorized to be universal for TQC. The source explains that the relationship between Fibonacci anyons and the quantum states is more intricate than with Majorana modes (Fibonacci anyons aren’t discussed in the paper).

Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.13547

The Paper: Physical Architecture to Theorized Idea

Part 1: The Architecture

The authors introduce a novel device architecture designed to enable single-shot interferometric measurement of fermion parity in a gate-defined superconducting nanowire.

◦ A gate-defined superconducting nanowire made from an InAs–Al heterostructure. If this nanowire is tuned into a one-dimensional topological superconductor (1DTS) state, it is expected to host Majorana zero modes (MZMs) at its ends. The nanowire is defined by a narrow Al strip and has separate plunger gates that control the density in five sections of the wire. The experiments discussed in the paper focus on one of these sections.

◦ The triple quantum dot interferometer (TQDI) consists of three electrostatically defined quantum dots that, together with a section of the nanowire, form a loop through which magnetic flux (Φ) can be controlled by varying the out-of-plane magnetic field (B⊥).

  • Two smaller dots (dot 1 and dot 3) act as tunable couplers, controlling the tunnel couplings (tL and tR) to the ends of the 1DTS section via tunnel couplings tm1, tm2.
  • A long quantum dot (dot 2) connects to dot 1 and dot 3 through tunnel couplings t12 and t23, respectively.
  • The quantum capacitance (CQ) of dot 2 is measured using dispersive gate sensing with an off-chip resonator circuit in a reflectometry setup. This measurement is the basis for determining the fermion parity.
  • An rf-based quantum dot–MZM tuning protocol was developed to balance the arms of the interferometer by measuring CQ while one of the small dots was maximally detuned. This allowed for μeV-level resolution in coupling extraction.

The overall design allows for a state-dependent shift of the quantum capacitance of the quantum dots (up to 1 fF) due to the coupling with the nanowire. The magnetic flux through the loop (controlled by B⊥) modulates this interaction, making the interferometer sensitive to the combined fermion parity of the dot–MZMs system.

Part 2: The Results

The researchers performed a sequence of consecutive quantum capacitance measurements to record time traces and study the dependence on the in-plane magnetic field (Bx). The key experimental findings include:
◦ The measured quantum capacitance (CQ∼) exhibited switches between two capacitance values, with a difference denoted as ΔCQ(Bx), which oscillated as a function of Bx.
◦ At certain Bx values, a clear random telegraph signal (RTS) was observed in CQ∼, particularly at the Bx corresponding to maximal ΔCQ(Bx).
◦ Histograms of the CQ∼ measurements showed a Bx-dependent bimodal distribution with peaks separated by ΔCQ(Bx).
◦ The oscillation period of ΔCQ(Bx) was 1.9 ± 0.1 mT, consistent with the expected flux of h/2e through the interference loop. The researchers interpret the RTS in CQ as originating from switches of the fermion parity in the wire.
◦ The time intervals between switches followed an exponential distribution with a characteristic time τRTS ≈ 2 ms. The dwell time in the two associated states was longer than 1 ms at in-plane magnetic fields of approximately 2T.
◦ A signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 1 in 3.6 μs was achieved at optimal flux values.
◦ These results enabled a parity measurement with an assignment error probability of 1% for an optimal measurement time.
◦ Quantum dynamics simulations, incorporating various noise sources and measurement backaction, showed good overall agreement with the experimental observations, supporting the interpretation of the results in terms of fermion parity switches.

While these measurements do not definitively prove the topological nature of the low-energy states, they strongly constrain the properties of any trivial Andreev bound state explanation, requiring the state to be at both ends of the wire and very weakly coupled to other low-energy fermionic states. The observed phenomena were reproducible across multiple measurements and a second device.

Conclusion:

According to the paper, this might prove useful in developing topological quantum computers that have a high likelihood of making up to the million qubit mark. Read the previous statement carefully and understand how the flow of logic works, the claims this paper made are all true but hidden behind major leaps of logic. Because yes, if this device architecture they propose works, then they could make a topological quantum computer but it isn’t apparent from the results yet! Apart from this, the “new state of matter” claim is also absolutely infuriating to me as claiming that discredits the work of Ettore Majorana and Alexei Kitaev as mentioned above. The topological superconductor isn’t a new state of matter but has already been theorized by the combined work of both these physicists.

So, according to me, it was already hyped up to a point of no return though, I do not condemn it. The quantum technology industry is slow at pace where strides are made once in a while rather than consistent progress which makes the market impatient and forces scientists to oversell their work however, the critiques to this paper aren’t limited to false or over-advertising but also the credibility of the paper. I am no scientist to comment on it though, knowing the paper is from Microsoft I don’t doubt underhanded tactics at play which all big companies are more than capable of and have been caught doing so. The results are condemned the most in all these critiques and have questioned the authenticity of Nature Journal as well which supposedly has high standards for others but this paper made the cut without maintaining its quality standards, by some scientists.

However, I love the Microsoft team who are working on topological quantum computing as my personal philosophy for quantum computing is similar to theirs; that there is a better way for quantum computing than superconducting qubits. I feel going the classical way is like limiting our creativity in the field and though half of the industry strives forward with it and it has proven its usability, I think if the other half focuses on long-term solutions like topological quantum computing or even better designs for quantum, we will reach our goal faster than we realize.
